(p.49); "stress in monomorphemic words is always final in the absence of heavy nuclei" (p.82); tone is treated separately as "predictable from the stress patterns of words and phrases" (p.89).

3941.heavy: Heavy nuclei = long vowels (v:) only; "Codas never count as heavy for the purposes of stress" (p.45 fn.9).
3941.prule: Primary stress on the rightmost heavy syllable (long-vowel nucleus) of the stem; if the stem has no heavy syllable, on the final (rightmost underlying) syllable. Unbounded, right-oriented; codas never count as heavy. Prefixes and class II suffixes are outside the stress domain; class I suffixes are inherently stressed and, being rightmost, take primary stress.
3941.srule: Storto 1999: no rhythmic secondary stress - iterative footing is 'not operative' and a monomorphemic word without long vowels has a single (final) stress (boroja 'snake'). Secondary stress only where a word holds more than one stressed unit: in root + class I (stressed) suffix words and in compounds, primary stress is on the stressed syllable of the rightmost morpheme and secondary stress on the stressed syllable of the leftmost morpheme (o.ky.'pa 'weapon' with secondary on ky; ko:.ko.t<o>.'pa 'bridge' with secondary on ko:); root + class II suffix words have primary stress only ('e.dna); every long-vowel nucleus is stressed, primary on the rightmost (pi:pi:p). Restated with F0 data in Storto & Demolin 2004. DISAGREEMENT: Everett 2006 reports rhythmic secondary stress on every other syllable preceding the final primary, unaffected by weight ((bo)(ro.'ja)), 'often on the same order of magnitude (in loudness)' as the primary.

tn.quote: Karitiana has a pitch accent system which assigns tone based on stress. ... After stress applies, a few tone assignment rules associate tonal melodies to certain stress prominent positions on the grid. ... Tones are a surface phenomenon in the language, predictable from the stress patterns of words and phrases. I will show that tone melodies are assigned to syllabic nuclei only after all stress rules have applied. Informally, the rules accounting for tone assignment are as follows. First, a H tone is assigned to the stress head of a morpheme, that is, to the nucleus that bears stress.

tn.locator: ch.2 sec.0 Introduction, p.79; ch.2 sec.2.1 'Stress-based tone rules', p.89
tn.note: Tone is not lexical: H sits on the stressed nucleus (rightmost heavy, else final), L elsewhere and at declarative ends, all derived from stress. Everett 2006 rejects the pitch-accent label.

evidence_works.detail: Syntax paper with no stress-placement statement. Stress enters only as a conditioning feature in morphophonological rules from the author's own field data: the declarative prefix takes the -ka- augment before 'a verb root with initial stress' (p.4, reprint pagination), ry- epenthesis rule (57) is conditioned on VRt [+Init stress, -Transitive] (p.12), and rule (75) 'prevents vowel clusters and contiguous stressed syllables between the positive response prefix and the following verb root' (pp.14-15); p.17 notes 'rising intonation on the final stressed syllable of the verb root' in imperatives. The verb roots that trigger -ka- in exx. (12)-(15) are monosyllabic (-tak- 'pound', -põn- 'hunt'), so initial stress there is also final; the polysyllabic roots -oky- 'kill' and -oty- 'bathe' take plain nã-/ta-, consistent with the entry's final-stress rule. Everett 2006:107-108, which the entry already cites, draws exactly this inference ('So Landin also refers indirectly to the position of word accent, at least in the case of verbs').

3942.dq: Stress is assigned to the root-final syllable of a word.
3942.dloc: Ch. 3, sec. 3.2.1 'Sound inventory, phonotactics and stress', pp. 40-41; scope statement sec. 3.2, p. 34 ('This section presents my phonological analysis of Kawahíva, based on the Juma and Jupaú dialects'); Karipuna listed as a Kawahíva dialect with glottocode kari1317 / ISO kuq in Table 2.4, p. 16 ('Karipuna 29 10 0 kari1317 kuq (Dos Santos 2017)'); oral/nasal contrast 'appears to be restricted to the root-final syllable, which coincides with the location of stress' p. 37.
3942.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable of the root ('Stress is assigned to the root-final syllable of a word'). The obligatory nominalizing enclitic =a on nouns is 'extrametrical' (author's term), so nouns surface with penultimate stress ([ñã.ˈndu.a] 'spider', [ta.pi.ˈʔi.ɾa] 'tapir') while bare verb forms surface with final stress ([ɛ.ˈpi], [ɛ.kɨ.ˈtʃi]); the negation circumfix nd(a)-...-i leaves stress on the root-final syllable ([nd-aĩˈmbɛ-i]); 'some suffixes trigger stress shift from the root-final syllable', the prose naming -ahim 'very' and -uhu 'aug' and citing exx. (15)-(16) (diminutive -ʔi) as evidence of shift in nouns. In every example the shifted stress lands on the final syllable of the suffix ([aĩmbɛ-aˈhĩm], [j-ipi-uˈhu], [vɨɾaˈʔia]), an observation from the examples, not a statement of the source. Position is set by morphological structure (root edge plus affix identity), not by syllable count from a word edge and not by weight.

3951.heavy: Stress-attracting ('heavy') = an OPEN syllable whose vowel is not /o/ (the reflex of *ɨ / schwa); closed syllables and syllables with /o/ are skipped, so the system counts open non-schwa syllables as heavy — the reverse of CVC-heavy. An open first syllable with a high vowel plus a homorganic glide (bi.jag, ʔu.wab) also repels stress. No vowel length contrast is invoked as the conditioning factor (length is a phonetic correlate of stress).
3951.dflt: final (last) syllable: ʔib.bog.’hul, ʔum.ʔal.’mot ('При отсутствии открытых слогов без /o/ ударение падает на последний слог')
3951.prule: Stress falls, as a rule, on the first (leftmost) open syllable whose vowel is not /o/ (the Yattuka reflex of *ɨ, i.e. the schwa-class vowel): ‘ba.ŋun, ʔuŋ.’ba.lon, qo.bob.’si.qa. If the word has no open syllable without /o/, stress falls on the last syllable: ʔib.bog.’hul, ʔum.ʔal.’mot. Roots whose open first syllable has a high vowel followed by a homorganic glide are stressed on the second syllable: bi’jag, ʔu’wab. Phonetic correlates: higher pitch and longer duration; intensity irrelevant.
3951.srule: No general secondary-stress rule; the §3.1.6 rule assigns one stress per word. Two identically marked (unranked) stresses per word are stated only for morphologically defined verb forms: DEP aspect forms of roots with /a/ in the first syllable are stressed on the 1st and 3rd syllables (ˈbu.mo.ˈŋun, ˈma.pi.ˈgut, ˈʔa.da.ˈlon, ˈʔi.ʔo.ˈna.mu.tan; some PFV/IMP forms follow the same template, ˈʔa.no.ˈmut, ʔim.ˈma.no.ˈmu.tan), and the uncounted stem-forming prefix paN-/pan- 'may carry secondary stress' (может нести вторичное ударение).

3956.prule: No Kerek-specific stress position is stated. Volodin says the prosodic organization of the word form obeys the same regularities as all Chukotko-Koryak languages and refers the reader to the Chukchi article of the same volume (Володин & Скорик 1997, pp. 23–39, now held); the only Kerek-specific observation is that prominence is realized as vowel lengthening (долготное выделение) whose position varies between syllables in the idiolects of individual speakers, with an explicit warning that broader conclusions are hard to draw. Vowel length is non-phonemic; there are no phonological tones. Examples: куниикаӈ 'you do/he does', мэккууникаӈ 'we (du.) do', ткуйааникаӈэӈ 'I want to do'. The cross-referenced Chukchi article (§2.1.2) rejects a dynamic-stress reading, describes a trochaic odd-syllable alternation in which even syllables are differently marked rather than unstressed, and says 'stress' is traditionally put on the 2nd syllable of trisyllables and the 1st of disyllables — not a single computable rule, and Koryak in the same volume (Жукова 1997: 'Ударением часто отмечен предпоследний слог. Ударение подвижное.') is described differently, so the deferral yields no Kerek position.

3960.prule: Prepausal Penultimate Lengthening (PPL): non-contrastive 'stress', assigned at the utterance level and realised as lengthening of the penultimate syllable of a pre-pausal neutral utterance (statements, non-urgent imperatives, citation forms). 3960.quote: Unlike the segmental elements and tone, stress in Qh is predictable always by rule, and never serves to differentiate lexical meanings or categories. A full-text search of the 49-page text for stress/accent/tone/tonal/pitch/prosod/register/emphas returns that single sentence. Every syllable in Table 1 and throughout the sketch carries a Chao pitch numeral (ŋʌ²¹, mi²¹, ʔo⁴⁴lo²², jʌ⁴², dok²²pʌ²², sum⁴³), i.e. pitch is recorded per syllable as lexical, not derived from a stress rule. Companion wordlist (Ikeda 2021, Basic Vocabulary, hdl:2433/263979) has no prose on accent (only hit: Matisoff 1972 'Loloish Tonal Split' in the abbreviations). Dorji 2022 (Himalayan Linguistics 21(2), p. 75 fn. 3) reads '(’) indicates a high register tone onset.' and is otherwise silent on word stress; the Bumthang-group relatives (Kurtoep, Bumthap; Michailovsky & Mazaudon 1994, pp. 546-547) have a high/low tone register tied to initial voicing. So the system is pitch/register-type; no source gives a stress rule.
